roles_compare.title: The Commons Conservators and The Friends: What’s the difference?
roles_compare.lede: Two separate organisations working together for the Commons.

conservators.title: The Commons Conservators
conservators.text: The Conservators have cared for and managed the Commons since the 1890 Tunbridge Wells Improvement Act. They are responsible for the practical management of the land, including byelaws, paths, woodland maintenance and tree safety, as well as employing the Warden and Ranger team. They are funded primarily through local council rates.

friends.title: Friends of the Commons
friends.text: Established in 1991, following the increased community interest in the Commons after the Great Storm of 1987, we are an independent local charity supporting the long-term protection and enjoyment of Tunbridge Wells and Rusthall Commons. We raise funds for projects on the Commons, organise volunteer sessions and nature-based events, and work alongside the Commons Conservators to care for this much-loved landscape.

visiting.heading: Visiting the Commons

items.title: Admission
items.description: Free and open to explore 365 days a year, with 256 acres of peaceful woodland, sandstone rocks and open glades for you to roam and enjoy.

items.title: Location
items.description: Tunbridge Wells and Rusthall Commons, Kent. The mainline railway station is just a 7-minute walk from the edge of the Commons.

items.title: Access
items.description: Waymarked footpaths link the town centre to Wellington Rocks, Toad Rock and Happy Valley.

items.title: Facilities
items.description: Free visitor parking bays on Fir Tree Road (TN4 8AH). Please take litter home.

campaign_story.title: Keeping the Commons in the hands of the people for generations to come
campaign_story.lede: The freehold of Tunbridge Wells and Rusthall Commons is currently on the open market. For over a century, the 1890 Tunbridge Wells Improvement Act has guaranteed public access, but ownership still matters. A private freeholder may have different priorities from those of the local community, particularly around access, land use, maintenance and the commercial use of the estate.
campaign_story.body:
Our philosophy is simple: this landscape belongs to everyone. We want people from near and far to walk beneath the towering Wellington Rocks, spot rare heathland wildlife, and feel the freedom that only ancient common land provides.

**Why community ownership matters:** Community ownership would give the Friends a long-term opportunity to keep the freehold in charitable ownership, with decisions guided by the protection and enjoyment of the Commons rather than commercial interests.

As a charity, the Friends are accountable to our members, trustees and the Charity Commission, with the protection, enhancement and public enjoyment of the Commons at the heart of our work. Over 3,000 residents and supporters have already pledged their backing.
campaign_story.quote_credit: Over 3,000 residents and supporters have pledged their backing
campaign_story.cta_note: Reported by The Guardian, BBC News and The Telegraph.

support_chapter.title: Take your place in protecting the commons
support_chapter.lede: The Friends are an independent, volunteer-led charity dedicated to caring for the Commons, funding conservation work, running guided community walks, and leading the historic bid to secure the 256-acre freehold in public ownership. Whether you donate, volunteer, join as an annual member or make a pledge, every contribution directly protects this precious landscape.
